name: GDPR consent banners and CMP prevalence — cookie/consent notices, the Consent Management Platforms (CMPs) that render them, the IAB Europe Transparency & Consent Framework (TCF) that some of them speak, and the automated dismissers built against them: Consent-O-Matic (Aarhus/CAVI), autoconsent (DuckDuckGo, also used by Brave), uBlock Origin's Annoyances/Cookie-notices lists, Brave's Cookiecrumbler, and the research prototype CookieEnforcer. Also called cookie banners, consent pop-ups, or consent interfaces.
kind: A regulatory regime (GDPR Art. 4(11)/7 plus ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3)), a commercial product category (CMPs), an industry standard (TCF), a body of measurement research, and a family of dismisser tools — five different kinds of thing that get discussed as one. Keeping them apart matters, because the prevalence numbers come from the research, the dismissal mechanics come from the tools, and the obligations come from the law, and none of the three transfers to the others.
maturity: Production and saturated. CMP adoption went from roughly 5% of sites pre-GDPR to about 42% by end-2023; a CHI 2025 cross-country study found CMPs account for at least 67% of all consent interfaces, corresponding to 44.5% of the websites it analysed. TCF is a mature but minority protocol — around 11.7% of detected CMPs expose the TCF API. The dismissers are mature and continuously maintained: Consent-O-Matic ships rules for over 200 CMPs, autoconsent is embedded in shipping browsers. CookieEnforcer remains a research prototype. Nothing here is going away; the regulatory direction of travel (and the EDPB's pressure on 'consent or pay' and on reject-button parity) is toward more standardised interfaces, not fewer.
license: Consent-O-Matic: GPL-family, open source, rule list separately maintained [uncertain — exact SPDX]. autoconsent: MPL-2.0/Apache-family, DuckDuckGo-maintained, open source [uncertain]. uBlock Origin filter lists: GPLv3 for the engine, with list-specific licensing for the annoyance lists. CookieEnforcer: academic prototype, licensing unclear [uncertain]. All are technically usable; the reason not to adopt them here is architectural rather than legal, as the ledger below sets out.
keeps_and_discards: As an obstacle, a consent interface both adds and subtracts content. It ADDS a modal document fragment — heading, body text, purpose descriptions, vendor lists (TCF vendor lists can run to hundreds of named companies and thousands of words), and several buttons — which a structure-agnostic fold will capture in full as ordinary page content, indistinguishable from the article it is covering. It SUBTRACTS by gating: many sites do not load main content, images, embeds or third-party media until consent is given, so the fold behind a banner is not merely the real page plus a banner, it is a reduced page plus a banner. A dismisser removes the added fragment and unlocks the subtracted content; leaving the banner in place preserves an honest but doubly-wrong capture. What a dismisser discards, in turn, is the evidence that a gate existed at all.
structure_preserved: The banner itself is ordinary DOM — usually a fixed-position div or dialog appended near the end of body, frequently inside a shadow root (OneTrust, Usercentrics and Cookiebot all use shadow DOM in at least some configurations), sometimes in an iframe. Nesting and order survive a fold normally. The shadow placement is the detail that matters most here: consent UI is one of the most common real-world uses of shadow DOM on the open web, so a project that reads composed shadow DOM will see these banners where a naive innerHTML reader would not, and a project that refuses closed roots will miss whichever of them use closed mode. Order is a specific hazard: a banner appended late in the document body but visually overlaying everything appears at the END of a layout-blind fold, which is exactly the wrong position — the SLM sees the article first and the interstitial last, in reverse of what a human perceives.
interactive_elements: Rich and adversarial. A banner presents between two and dozens of controls: Accept All, Reject All (present on the first layer only about half the time in EU-facing samples), Manage Preferences, per-purpose toggles, per-vendor toggles, and legitimate-interest switches that are frequently pre-enabled. Dark patterns are the norm rather than the exception — asymmetric button styling, reject buried behind extra clicks, pre-ticked boxes, and interface interference are documented at scale. Consent interfaces are therefore the single hardest case for a 'tag plus interactivity' representation: the tags and interactivity are entirely ordinary (button, input[type=checkbox], role=dialog) while the semantics are the whole point, and no amount of tag-level fidelity conveys that one button consents to 800 vendors and the adjacent one does not.
interactive_state_fidelity: This is where consent UI stresses the project's central bet hardest, and it is worth being precise. The states that matter — which toggles are pre-checked, which are disabled, which section is aria-expanded, whether a control is aria-hidden behind a scrim — are exactly the states that encode the dark pattern, and they are exactly what markdown drops and the accessibility tree keeps. A pre-ticked legitimate-interest toggle and an unticked one render as identical markdown text; only checked/aria-checked distinguishes them. So 'tag plus interactivity' earns its keep here decisively IF it carries the state, and fails completely if it carries only the tag. The token cost is real but bounded — a state suffix on interactive nodes only, and interactive nodes are a small fraction of any page. The harder cost is that a full TCF preference panel with several hundred vendor toggles is a genuine budget event: hundreds of near-identical stateful rows that carry almost no information individually. That argues for a per-address collapse rule on runs of structurally identical stateful siblings, which is a size-and-repetition heuristic rather than a structure classifier and so stays inside the constraints.
layout_awareness: The fold reads none, and this item is the sharpest illustration of what that costs. A consent banner is defined by rendering: fixed position, high z-index, full-viewport scrim, overlaying content. Every one of those properties is invisible to a layout-blind fold, which sees a div of text and buttons somewhere near the end of body — structurally unremarkable. This is precisely why CookieEnforcer, the one research system that detects notices WITHOUT per-CMP CSS selectors, does so by using the rendering pattern of HTML elements: having given up selectors, it had to buy detection back with geometry. That trade is the empirical core of the third tension and it recurs below.
javascript_required: Almost always. Modern CMPs inject their UI from script — OneTrust, Usercentrics, Cookiebot, Quantcast and Sourcepoint all render client-side, frequently into a shadow root and sometimes after a deliberate delay. A no-script fetch of many sites therefore returns a page with no banner and, often, no gating either, which is a genuinely interesting asymmetry: reading with scripts disabled sometimes yields MORE content than reading with them enabled. That is not an option for this project, which needs composed shadow DOM from a live browser, and it means every capture of an EU-facing commercial page fires the CMP and the consent-conditional tracker load along with it.
evaluation_method: The prevalence research is crawl-based and reasonably rigorous: automated crawls from multiple geographic vantage points, per-site CMP detection (usually by script-URL and DOM signature matching), classification of button presence and layer depth, and in the better studies a manual-coded validation subsample. The CHI 2025 cross-country work explicitly studies the scraping methodology as a contribution, which is unusual and welcome. Compliance research adds legal coding by trained annotators against GDPR/ePrivacy criteria, and behavioural work adds field experiments on real users. The dismisser tools are 'evaluated' almost entirely by issue tracker — a rule breaks, someone files it, the rule is fixed — which is maintenance, not measurement, and no dismisser publishes a coverage figure against a random sample of the web.
corpus_size_and_origins: The figures are strong on scale and weak on denominator discipline, and the project's own working number needs correcting. The commonly-quoted '67% of top sites show a consent interface' does not match the source it appears to derive from: the CHI 2025 study reports that at least 67% of all CONSENT INTERFACES are CMPs, corresponding to 44.5% of the WEBSITES analysed. Those are different claims with different denominators, and the safer statement is that roughly 40–50% of measured sites present a consent interface, with the fraction rising steeply for EU-facing commercial sites and falling to near zero for documentation, archives and government pages. Other anchors: ~5% CMP adoption pre-GDPR rising to ~42% by end-2023; ~11.7% of CMPs exposing the TCF API; only 11.8–15% of banners meeting minimal legal requirements depending on the criteria used; over 60% of CMP-using sites setting trackers before consent. Crucially, every one of these is measured from an EU or EU-simulated vantage point on top-list sites — prevalence is strongly location-dependent (the same site shows different or no notice outside the EU), and top-list sampling over-represents exactly the commercial archetype where banners cluster.
reported_precision_recall: For the prevalence research, detection precision is high (CMP script signatures are distinctive) and recall is the soft spot — bespoke, self-rolled banners on sites not using a commercial CMP are systematically under-detected, which biases every prevalence figure DOWNWARD, in the opposite direction to the top-list sampling bias. For the dismissers, no precision/recall is published by anyone. Consent-O-Matic's coverage is stated as 200+ CMPs, which is a coverage count and not a rate; the honest inference from the CMP market's shape is that a few dozen platforms cover the large majority of CMP-using sites, so 200+ rules probably reach a high share of CMP-fronted pages and approximately none of the bespoke long tail. CookieEnforcer reports accuracy figures for its notice detection and action prediction on its own evaluation set [uncertain — specific numbers not verified], and it is the only member of the family that reports anything at all.
independent_oracle: For prevalence, yes and it is decent: manual annotation of subsamples is independent of the automated detector, and cross-country crawls provide a natural control (a site that shows a banner from an EU IP and not from a US one confirms the detector is reading a real behaviour rather than an artifact). For legal compliance, the oracle is human legal judgement, which is independent of the crawler but not reproducible between annotators, and inter-annotator agreement is rarely reported. For the dismissers, there is no oracle at all — a rule 'works' when nobody complains, which is silent failure institutionalised. That absence is the strongest reason to distrust any claim about dismisser coverage.
evidence_independence: Better than most items in this research set. The prevalence and dark-pattern literature is academic and peer-reviewed (CHI, PoPETs, USENIX), from multiple independent groups across several countries, and is frequently critical of the industry it measures. The dismissers are independent of the CMPs. The self-interested evidence lives on the other side: CMP vendors publish consent-rate statistics designed to sell CMPs, and those numbers should not be mixed with the academic ones. IAB Europe's own TCF materials are advocacy. The one structural weakness is that most of the academic work shares a small set of crawling toolchains, so a systematic blind spot in the tooling — bespoke banners, shadow-DOM-hidden banners, delayed injection — would propagate across studies without being caught.
page_archetype_coverage: Sharply differentiated and the differentiation is more useful than the aggregate. Consent interfaces cluster on news and media, e-commerce, travel, and any archetype monetised by advertising; they are rare on documentation, public archives, government, and academic sites. TCF specifically is an advertising framework and is therefore concentrated almost entirely in ad-monetised publishers. For this project the practical reading is that a corpus of archive and documentation pages will encounter banners at a rate far below the headline 40–50%, and a corpus of commercial pages will encounter them on nearly every EU-facing origin. Reporting a single 'fraction of captures gated' across a mixed corpus averages two populations that behave completely differently, and the project should report it per archetype — which it can do without a classifier, by grouping on origin rather than on inferred page type.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Locale is the dominant variable in the entire item, more so than in anything else researched here. Whether a banner appears at all, which buttons it offers, and whether reject is on the first layer are all functions of the requesting IP's jurisdiction and the Accept-Language header; a site shows a full GDPR interface to an EU vantage point, a CCPA 'Do Not Sell' link to a Californian one, and nothing to much of the rest of the world. Banner text is served in the site's locale, so a fold of a non-English site captures the banner in that language, and any keyword-based recognition would need per-language vocabularies — another reason the dismissers use selectors rather than text. CJK and RTL banners are structurally identical and textually opaque to English heuristics. Any measurement of gating rate must therefore record the egress jurisdiction, or it is uninterpretable.
leaks_outward: Substantial, and much of it happens before any choice is made. Loading a CMP-fronted page contacts the CMP vendor (OneTrust, Cookiebot, Usercentrics, Sourcepoint, Quantcast) which sees the request; over 60% of CMP-using sites set trackers before consent is given, so third-party disclosure typically occurs regardless. Accepting a TCF banner authorises data flow to the vendor list, which routinely runs to several hundred named companies. Rejecting reduces but does not eliminate it. For this project the direct consequence is that the measured 3,082 external requests to 92+ hosts per corpus run is partly a consent-mediated number: the request count would differ between accept, reject, and no-interaction runs, and the project does not currently record which of those states its captures were taken in — meaning that headline figure is an average over an unrecorded variable.
mechanism_detectability: The banner does not detect the reader; the CMP infrastructure around it partly does. Concretely deployed and worth naming: CMPs write consent state to cookies and localStorage (euconsent-v2 for TCF, OptanonConsent for OneTrust, CookieConsent for Cookiebot), so a browser arriving with a fresh profile every time is visibly a first-time visitor on every visit — an easy, cheap, universally-available signal that a site with any bot logic can read, and one that fresh-profile-per-run discipline makes unavoidable. That is a real and under-appreciated tension between the privacy-preserving choice (fresh profile, no cross-run linkage) and the low-detectability choice (persistent profile with plausible consent history). More aggressively, several CMPs and anti-adblock vendors detect whether the banner was dismissed WITHOUT a genuine interaction — checking for the isTrusted flag on the click event, or for consent state changing without a corresponding user gesture — and this is actively deployed in anti-adblock-adjacent products, which is precisely how autoconsent-style dismissal gets caught. Both signals are simple property or event reads, in production today, not theoretical. Neither is affected by anything in the fold; both are actuator-layer facts. Nothing in this item bears on the attachShadow question except tangentially: because CMPs are among the heaviest real-world users of shadow DOM, a project that reads composed shadow roots gets consent UI 'for free', which is an argument that the open-root reading capability is doing real work.
countermeasures: Four options and only the last two survive the constraints. (1) Rule-list dismissal — Consent-O-Matic, autoconsent, uBO annoyance lists. (2) Cosmetic hiding without interaction — uBO's element-hiding, which removes the visual banner but does not consent, so gated content stays gated and the fold is left in a partially-honest state that is arguably the worst of both worlds. (3) Jurisdictional avoidance — reading from a vantage point where no banner is shown, which sidesteps the problem by trading it for a different corpus (you are now reading a different page than an EU user would). (4) Record and accept — take the capture with the banner present, record 'consent-gated, no interaction' as gate state, and treat the gated content as genuinely absent. Option 4 is the only one that is both constraint-respecting and honest, and it is what this item recommends.
measured_fidelity_cost: The number the project needs here does not exist in the literature and is directly measurable with the existing harness. What the local measurements already establish is suggestive: the 10.49% block_trackers cost on live sites against 0.16% on saved pages is precisely the shape a consent-gating effect would take, because tracker blocking and consent refusal suppress overlapping request populations, and saved pages have neither. It is therefore likely that some fraction of that 10.49% is not 'hardening cost' at all but consent-conditional content that never loaded. The experiment to separate them is a three-arm run on the same live URLs — no interaction, dismissed-by-rule, and accepted — with fold size and content overlap compared against the 0.07% null floor. If the accept arm recovers content that the no-interaction arm lacks, the gap is the true cost of the honest posture, and it should be reported as a gate-state effect in its own ledger rather than folded into hardening cost. Predicting the sign: on ad-monetised pages the gap will be large; on documentation and archive pages, near zero.
gate_state_at_capture: This item is the reason the field exists, and it supplies the constraint-respecting answer to the third tension. Recording gate state does not require identifying a banner. Four layout-free, structure-agnostic signals are available and cheap: (a) presence of a known CMP script origin in the request log — an address-keyed peripheral observation, not a DOM classifier, and it identifies the CMP vendor precisely because CMP script URLs are distinctive; (b) presence of a CMP consent cookie or localStorage key, likewise address-keyed by name; (c) presence of the __tcfapi function on window, which is a standardised global that TCF CMPs must expose and that answers 'is there a TCF consent gate here' with one property read and no structural inference at all; (d) fold-size delta between a no-interaction capture and a prior or parallel capture of the same URL. None of these names a region, none reads geometry, and together they cover the CMP-fronted majority. The bespoke long tail escapes all four, and should be recorded as unknown rather than guessed at.
determinism: Poor and worse than it looks. The same URL fetched twice from the same machine can yield: a banner (fresh profile), no banner (consent cookie present), a different banner (A/B tested — CMPs routinely run consent-rate experiments), or a delayed banner that appears after the fold was taken. Banner injection timing is a genuine race, and a fold taken at DOMContentLoaded versus one taken two seconds later can differ by an entire modal. This is a substantial and under-recognised source of run-to-run fold variance on live commercial pages, and it is plausibly a component of the gap between the 0.07% saved-page floor and live-site variance. Any determinism claim measured only on saved pages is silent about it.
determinism_across_versions: The banners drift continuously — CMP vendors redesign, and regulatory pressure (the EDPB's cookie-banner taskforce, national DPA enforcement on reject-button parity) forces periodic redesigns across whole vendor customer bases at once. That is the specific reason selector-based dismissers require constant maintenance: a single OneTrust UI change breaks one rule across tens of thousands of sites simultaneously. Detection by script origin and by __tcfapi presence is far more stable than detection by DOM shape, which is another argument for the address-keyed signals above.
reproducibility: Weak. A capture of an EU-facing commercial page is not reproducible without recording jurisdiction, profile state, consent state, and capture timing relative to banner injection. None of the prevalence studies publishes its raw captures, and the sites themselves change. For this project's own corpus the implication is concrete: saved pages are reproducible and live pages are not, and the difference is largely attributable to this item plus anti-bot differentiation. That is a good reason to keep the saved corpus as the determinism baseline while being explicit that it understates live variance — which the 0.16%-versus-10.49% split already demonstrates.
failure_modes: For the fold: a banner captured as ordinary content, at the wrong position (late in document order despite visually dominating), with gated content silently missing. For dismissers: rule staleness after a CMP redesign; wrong action taken (accepting when the user configured reject, which is a consent-integrity failure with legal weight, not just a bug); dismissal detected as non-genuine via isTrusted checks; and inability to handle the bespoke tail. For CookieEnforcer's approach: dependence on rendering, which fails on any page whose layout it misreads and which is unavailable to a layout-blind system by definition. For the whole category: the 'consent or pay' and login-wall variants, which are not dismissible at all and which conflate the consent gate with a paywall.
failure_visibility: Silent in every direction, and this is the item's most serious property. A banner-gated capture returns HTTP 200 with well-formed HTML and a plausible token count; nothing signals that half the page never loaded. A dismisser that clicks the wrong button reports success. A banner that appeared after the fold was taken leaves no trace. There is no error, no exception, no status code. The only defences are the positive gate-state signals listed above and cross-capture comparison — which makes this the clearest case in the research set for the project's standing refusal of silent degradation being operationally, not just philosophically, necessary.
scale_limits: Rule-list dismissal scales badly in maintenance rather than in compute: 200+ CMP rules is a permanent human-labour commitment that grows with the CMP market and churns with every vendor redesign, and no amount of engineering reduces it. Detection by script origin or __tcfapi scales at constant cost per page with no maintenance. Prevalence crawling scales linearly in sites but must be repeated per jurisdiction, multiplying cost by the number of vantage points, which is why cross-country studies are rare and valuable.
delta_cost_model: Banner injection is a well-behaved delta in principle — a subtree appended near the end of body — and an O(delta) sensor should absorb it cheaply. Three cases fall outside: injection into a shadow root, where the mutation is observed only if the root is open and observed; consent-conditional content unlocking, which is not a local delta at all but a page-wide reload or a large-scale insertion across many subtrees at once; and CSS-only banner reveal, where the DOM does not change and only computed style does, which a DOM-mutation-driven delta model cannot see by construction. The third is the one worth naming explicitly in the project's out-of-model change list, because it is common (banners pre-rendered hidden and revealed by class toggle) and it is exactly the class the no-layout constraint makes invisible.
reanchoring_stability: Consent state changes node identity in bulk: accepting a banner can cause a page to load embeds, lazy images and third-party widgets that shift sibling indices throughout the document, breaking raw-xpath anchors far from the banner itself. This is a strong argument for content-hash-assisted re-anchoring over pure positional xpath, and for treating a large simultaneous anchor-failure event as a gate transition rather than as drift — the same discriminator that distinguishes challenge-page substitution. The trie's content component earns its place here specifically.
adversarial_exposure: Consent banners are not themselves adversarial in the injection sense, but they contribute two things to the second tension. First, they are a large, high-volume source of text that is visually secondary and structurally indistinguishable from primary content to a layout-blind fold — not concealed, but mis-weighted, which for an SLM is a related failure. Second, they establish that a substantial fraction of real-world 'invisible to the human' content is invisible for rendering reasons that have nothing to do with adversarial intent: pre-rendered-but-hidden banners, hidden preference panels behind a Manage button, and collapsed vendor lists are all present in the DOM and absent from the human's view. Any measurement of what fraction of concealment is addressable without geometry must count these as the benign majority of the DOM-present-but-unseen population, which they are — and which means the adversarial fraction of hidden content is smaller than raw hidden-node counts suggest, in the project's favour.
provenance_carrying: Banners carry no provenance and destroy some: consent-conditional content that loads after acceptance arrives with no marker distinguishing it from content that was always present. What the project should record per capture, in the peripheral, is a compact consent tuple — CMP vendor (from script origin, if any), __tcfapi present (boolean), consent cookie present (boolean), interaction taken (none/accepted/rejected/dismissed), and egress jurisdiction. That is five fields, none of which requires reading document structure, and together they make a capture's gate state reconstructible after the fact, which it currently is not.
roundtrip_safety: Banner text is ordinary prose and roundtrips normally. One narrow hazard: TCF vendor lists and purpose descriptions contain long runs of company names with punctuation, ampersands and occasional markup-like characters, and a naive markdown serialisation of hundreds of such rows is a plausible place for escaping bugs to hide — high volume, low salience, nobody reads it. If the project uses roundtrip stability as an oracle-free fidelity metric, consent panels are a good stress case precisely because they are repetitive and unloved.
token_budget_and_ordering: A consent interface is a budget hazard out of proportion to its value. A simple banner is a few hundred tokens; an expanded TCF preference panel with several hundred vendor toggles can be thousands, all near-duplicate, all of essentially zero informational worth to the task at hand. And the ordering is actively wrong: a late-in-body banner lands at the END of a document-order fold, which past 50% context fill is the recency-dominant, highest-attention region — so the least valuable content in the capture occupies the most valuable position. Two remedies stay inside the constraints: collapse runs of structurally identical stateful siblings with a count (a repetition heuristic, not a region classifier), and surface gate state as an explicit early marker so the model knows the document is gated rather than having to infer it from a wall of vendor names at the end.
representation_cost: Highly variable: tens of tokens for a dismissed or absent banner, a few hundred for a simple one, low thousands for an expanded TCF panel. What is lost per token saved by collapsing vendor lists is close to nothing for almost every task, and everything for the narrow task of auditing what a site's consent panel actually offers — which argues for collapsing by default with the full content retained in the peripheral, addressable by key, rather than discarded.
what_could_be_adopted: Three things, and one explicit refusal. Adopt: (1) the four layout-free gate-state signals — CMP script origin in the request log, consent cookie/localStorage key by name, __tcfapi presence on window, and fold-size delta — as the constraint-respecting substitute for banner detection; (2) the three-arm live measurement (no interaction / dismissed / accepted) to decompose the existing 10.49% live cost into hardening cost and consent-gating cost, which the current single number conflates; (3) the repetition-collapse rule for runs of structurally identical stateful siblings, which addresses the token blow-up without naming any region. Refuse: rule-list dismissal, for the reasons in the ledger. Also worth internalising is the corrected prevalence framing — roughly 40–50% of measured sites present a consent interface, heavily archetype- and jurisdiction-dependent, not a flat 67%.
constraint_violation_ledger: This item settles the third tension, and the answer is: CONFIRMED, with one instructive near-miss. Every practical dismisser is a structure classifier. Consent-O-Matic's rule list is explicitly a JSON structure of per-CMP detectors and methods built on CSS selectors, with a DOM selection mechanism for targeting elements — 200+ named CMPs, each with hand-written selectors. autoconsent has the same architecture. uBO and Brave annoyance lists are cosmetic filter rules, which are CSS selectors by definition. Brave's Cookiecrumbler automates the GENERATION of such rules but still emits rules. The near-miss is CookieEnforcer, the one system that deliberately avoids per-CMP selectors — and it detects notices using the RENDERING PATTERN of HTML elements, i.e. it pays for structure-agnosticism with geometry. That is the finding: across the whole family, banner dismissal is purchased either with a structure classifier or with layout, and no member does it with neither. Per constraint: structure_agnosticism — all selector-based dismissers REJECTED; they are region classifiers naming 'the consent dialog'. no_layout_in_the_fold — CookieEnforcer REJECTED for the fold, ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY in principle, since an actuator may read geometry, though adopting it would mean the actuator carries a rendering-based classifier that the fold must never consult. o_delta — the dismissers are event-driven and cheap per page, no violation, but CSS-only banner reveal is an out-of-model change class that must be enumerated. no_mocks — no violation; dismissers act on the real page, though clicking Accept on a real consent dialog is a legally meaningful act, not a test fixture, which is a different objection. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed — a real coverage limit rather than a violation: CMPs are heavy shadow-DOM users, so closed-root banners are unreachable by any dismisser and by this project's fold alike, and both fail the same way. CONSTRAINT-RESPECTING OPTION, stated plainly: do not dismiss. Record the gated state using the four signals above, capture the page faithfully as gated, mark the capture's gate state in the peripheral, and treat consent-locked content as genuinely absent rather than as something to be extracted by defeating the gate. This costs content — measurably, and the measurement is worth running — and it buys constraint integrity, legal defensibility, and an honest corpus in which gated and ungated captures are distinguishable rather than silently mixed.
governance_signal_handling: Consent banners are the user-facing half of the same governance question that robots.txt, ai.txt and AIPREF address machine-side, and they interact awkwardly. A consent interface is an expression of the site's position on data processing directed at humans; an automated reader clicking Accept is generating consent that no human gave, which is not merely legally void but is arguably a misrepresentation to the site. Clicking Reject is more defensible but still fabricates a user act. Taking no action and recording the gate is the only option that does not manufacture a legal fiction. There is no machine-readable consent-preference channel analogous to robots.txt — no way for an agent to say 'I am not a data subject, serve me the ungated page' — and that gap is real. Web Bot Auth plus AIPREF is the closest thing to a future path: an identified agent could, in principle, be served content under a declared basis rather than under a consent fiction. Nothing like that exists today.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The most legally loaded item in the privacy category. Automated interaction with a consent dialog is not a neutral technical act: GDPR Art. 4(11) requires consent to be a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the DATA SUBJECT'S wishes, and a script clicking Accept satisfies none of those — the consent recorded is invalid, and the site is now processing on a basis it believes it has and does not. That exposes the site, not only the agent, which is an unusual and uncomfortable position to put a publisher in. Clicking Reject is far safer but still simulates a subject's act. Under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, where the persistent storage of scraped content is the regulated act and legitimate interest turns on reasonable expectations and respect for expressed preferences, content obtained by manufacturing consent is materially harder to defend than content served ungated. On PII: consent-gated content skews toward personalised and user-generated material, so defeating the gate raises the personal-data density of the corpus at the same time as it weakens the lawful basis for storing it — the two risks compound rather than trade off. The recommendation follows directly and is the same as the constraint recommendation: no interaction, record the gate, accept the hole.
